items.title: $10.8K M5 Ultra Mac Studio benchmark shows a 6x increase in multi-core compute since M1
items.summary: Apple Silicon was a gamble, and in spite of repeated reports of brain drains and executive exodus, the M5 Ultra is Apple's most powerful chipset by a long shot.
items.content_html:
Apple Silicon was a gamble, and in spite of repeated reports of brain drains and executive exodus, the M5 Ultra is Apple's most powerful chipset by a long shot.

Earlier Tuesday, the M6 benchmarks showed up on Geekbench with impressive results. It is expected to be the only chipset in that generation, so the M5 Ultra is the high-end pros will have to work with for the time being.

Another Geekbench result showed up, this time for the M5 Ultra. The 36-core CPU Mac Studio with 256GB of RAM scored 3,774 in single-core and 52,516 in multi-core.

Geekbench is a useful reference tool for generalized performance gains, not one that determines real-world use. However, the numbers don't lie, and Apple's M5 Ultra is an incredible chipset.

For comparison, the M6 scored 4,071 in single-core and 22,783 in multi-core. That single-core score makes since given it is the new 2nm package with more powerful cores.

The multi-core results show the 36-core M5 Ultra scores more than double the 12-core M6.

M5 Ultra 3,774 single-core and 52,516 multi-core in Geekbench

Compare the M5 Ultra to the original M1 chip and you can see just how far Apple Silicon has come in six years. The M1 in a MacBook Air got a single-core score of 2,150 and a multi-core score of 8,434.

That means M5 Ultra is about 6x more performant in multi-core processes versus M1.

Moore's Law is well and completely dead, but that hasn't stopped Apple from finding notable performance gains with each chip generation. The move to Apple Silicon was met with some concern, but it has proven to be an incredible success for the company.

Meanwhile, in spite of the advances over time, concerns continue to creep up over Apple's ability to maintain that success. Reports keep coming out about so-called "brain drain" and the attempted exit of chip mastermind Johny Srouji.

Instead, Apple continues to develop industry-leading processors that sip on power. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio starts at $5,499, while the configuration in this benchmark is $10,799.

Shipments are highly constrained, especially for the higher-end models. Customers can expect to get an M5 Ultra Mac Studio between November 9 and sometime in January, depending on configuration options.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro review roundup: great cameras, no surprises, isn't iPhone Duo
items.summary: The first reviews of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are out and without exception, they say it's unfairly overshadowed by the iPhone Duo.
items.content_html:
The first reviews of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are out and without exception, they say it's unfairly overshadowed by the iPhone Duo.

Pre-orders for the iPhone 18 Pro models appeared to get off to a slow start, at least compared to how shipping was rapidly delayed for the iPhone 17 Pro. But now that reviewers are getting to test it in the real world, there is only one criticism.

"Is it expensive?" asks Marques Brownlee in his YouTube review. "Hell, yeah."

He also describes it as what Apple would previously have called an S release, a refinement to the preceding model. "I think it's tempting to be disappointed by that, but after using it for the past week, I actually think it's underrated," he continued.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

"If there was a big tick in the tick/tock cycle of update [with the iPhone 17 Pro redesign] then this is a pretty good tock update," says Brownlee. "The 2nm chip is doing a lot of the heavy lifting here and the variable aperture camera it's subtle if anything but it has potential future value as cameras evolve."

Doesn't fold

"It might not fold in half, but everything else about the iPhone 18 Pro remains elite," writes Robert Leedham in a GQ review headlined "Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is still king of the camera phones."

Describing it as "the iPhone you're probably going to settle for" instead of the $2,000 iPhone Duo, Leedham concentrates on the new camera updates. "Really this expanded aperture is for photographers who know how to use it," he says.

"In many respects, the iPhone 18 Pro is a deliberately low-key release from Apple," he concludes. "All the shine is meant to be on the iPhone Duo this year, and so none of the Pro's upgrades are remotely extravagant."

"For now, I'll happily settle for the Pro's routine excellence," says Leedham, "it's elite in every respect."

Camera improvements for all

Mashable disagrees about the camera upgrades only being for professional users. "Even if you're not a pro, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max take excellent photographs," says its review.

It does say that the iPhone Duo is "the more intriguing model" of Apple's new lineup, though, and also that it isn't a necessary upgrade for iPhone 17 Pro users. "If you have an even older model," it says, "the 18 Pro will be a massive upgrade, especially when it comes to battery life."

The Verge takes a middle ground, agreeing that the camera updates are for all users, but not that they are remarkable. "The Pro's camera upgrade offers minor image quality improvements," it says, "whether or not you know what an f-stop is."

Just as all reviewers also talk about the iPhone Duo, most conclude that the iPhone 18 Pro is the more practical buy. But Mashable isn't as sure as the others.

"It's a tough call at this point," its review says. "If you're not sure, maybe wait until you can actually try the Duo in person."

Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo start on October 16, 2026. The first models will ship by October 23, which is also when it will appear in Apple Stores.

items.title: New in iOS 27.2 beta: redesigned Health app, Siri AI localization, more
items.summary: Apple's redesigned Health app has already reached developers and testers with the first beta of iOS 27.2. Here's what's new.
items.content_html:
Apple's redesigned Health app has already reached developers and testers with the first beta of iOS 27.2. Here's what's new.

On Wednesday, following the full public release of iOS 27, Apple made iOS 27.2 beta 1 available to all compatible devices except the iPhone Duo. Apple's first foldable phone is expected to ship with iOS 27.1, while the remainder of the iPhone lineup will receive iOS 27.2

The first developer beta of iOS 27.2 includes a redesigned Health app, which Apple previewed at its "Surprise and Shine" event on September 9. Initially available only in U.S. English, the new Health app offers Apple Intelligence insights, along with a new Longevity Tab and a Readiness score.

Apple said that it will not ship with iOS 27.2, however. They have also said that it will arrive before the end of 2026.

Apple's redesigned Health app will work alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12, which include improved health sensing systems. For instance, users will be able to use their iPhone and Apple Watch together to complete health-related tests and activities, like VO2 Max evaluations.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

With Wednesday's iOS 27.2 developer beta, Apple has also improved Siri AI localization. The virtual assistant is now available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, albeit only in beta for the time being.

Additionally, iOS 27.2 beta 1 enables dual capture for group FaceTime calls, meaning users will be able to share video feeds from both front-facing and rear iPhone cameras. The feature itself isn't new, as Apple highlighted it during the launch of the iPhone 17 range, but it was previously limited to standard FaceTime calls.

Separately, Apple TV profiles, introduced with tvOS 26.2, are now available on the iPhone. Those running the first iOS 27.2 developer beta can add existing Apple TV profiles or create new ones. The feature itself is entirely optional, though.

Overall, iPhone users, and especially those with an Apple Watch, are in for a substantial upgrade with iOS 27.2. With a redesigned Health app, better language support for Siri AI, and dual capture now being available in group FaceTime calls, there's a lot to look forward to.

items.title: Three photographers put the iPhone 18 Pro camera to work
items.summary: Apple is putting the iPhone 18 Pro into the hands of three acclaimed photographers to see what its redesigned camera system is capable of.
items.content_html:
Apple is putting the iPhone 18 Pro into the hands of three acclaimed photographers to see what its redesigned camera system is capable of.

Announced at September's "Surprise and Shine" event, Apple's iPhone 18 Pro brings several changes to the iPhone camera system. These include a variable aperture and improved low-light photography.

As with previous iPhone generations, Apple has handed the device to professional photographers to demonstrate what its cameras can produce.

Apple's latest Shot on iPhone project is "What Holds Us," a photography exhibition featuring work shot entirely on iPhone 18 Pro. The exhibition includes work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin.

Kathy Ryan, former New York Times Magazine photography director, curated the exhibition. It centers around the theme of human connection.

"What Holds Us" opens in New York City on September 18 and runs through September 20. Apple says the exhibition will later travel to London and Shanghai.

Jimmy Chin

Jimmy Chin is a climber, adventure photographer, and Academy Award-winning filmmaker known for documenting people in extreme environments. For the exhibition, Chin photographed climbers in British Columbia's Bugaboo Mountains.

"I've always been interested in human passion and meaning, and where that intersects with the raw beauty of wild landscapes," explains Chin. "When you spend a lot of time in these places, you start to look at things differently. You start to see the details."

Image credit: Jimmy Chin via Apple

He used the iPhone 18 Pro for close-ups, action shots, and large panoramas while working in the mountains.

Utilizing an iPhone, effectively a point-and-shoot camera, allowed Chin to carry less while working in difficult conditions. This was a huge boon for both practicality and safety, as during Chin's time on the mountain, winds reached up to 70 miles per hour.

Jack Davison

Jack Davison is a portrait photographer and director known for high-contrast images using strong blacks and whites. His work for "What Holds Us" focuses on people interacting with clay and chalk.

Image credit: Jack Davison via Apple

"I genuinely was blown away by the camera on iPhone 18 Pro," Davison notes. "There was something about the quality of the imagery that felt like a huge leap. Not just from a technical standpoint, but in its ability to create more artistic and surreal images."

The resulting images are visceral, with subjects covered in clay as they themselves become human sculptures. Ryan was particularly impressed with the contrasts, highlights, and shadows Davison achieved without a darkroom.

Alex Prager

Alex Prager is known for staged, cinematic photographs that often feature large groups of people and heavily constructed scenes. Her work for the exhibition combined overhead crowd scenes with tighter portraits of individual subjects.

Prager used the iPhone 18 Pro's camera system to move between those perspectives while shooting on a Los Angeles soundstage.

Image credit: Alex Prager via Apple

"Photography has changed a lot, and this particular camera is more like a video stream, in essence, which also shapes how we approach images today — more like video with higher output in our photo albums and on social media," Prager explains.

"It was exciting for me to think about all of this while harking back to a timeless crowd winding down from a celebration."

Ryan believes that Prager's method of working showed what the iPhone 18 Pro was capable of.

"She was able to take advantage of iPhone's ease of use and adaptability while also maintaining the high production values seen on a major film set," Ryan said.

items.title: John Ternus' iPhone Duo got a red carpet moment, cue internet drama
items.summary: Apple CEO John Ternus whipped out his iPhone Duo on the Emmys red carpet, to the delight of the press gaggle. The Internet immediately started whining, as it does.
items.content_html:
Apple CEO John Ternus whipped out his iPhone Duo on the Emmys red carpet, to the delight of the press gaggle. The Internet immediately started whining, as it does.

The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards were a big success for Apple TV. As the new CEO of Apple, John Ternus was in attendance, and he used the opportunity of a red carpet interview to flash the iPhone Duo in front of the cameras.

In a clip posted by Deadline to X, Ternus reaches into his tuxedo, pulls out the iPhone Duo, and opens it up. After a squeal of delight from the reporter, the grinning Ternus folds the iPhone Duo up and puts it back in his pocket.

While the reporter was obviously happy to see the device in person, the Internet was not.

Internet peanut gallery

Comments below the post included a lot of discussion about Ternus, but quite a few about the iPhone Duo itself. Chiefly that it had a seemingly bad display.

"That matte screen is so bad it's making me think about getting a Fold 8," one person writes. "The quality of inner screen so suck" another bashes out along with emojis of a sad face.

Apple CEO John Ternus shows the new iPhone Duo | #Emmys pic.twitter.com/7a6Rp1yMSS

— Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 14, 2026

Others touched on how you couldn't see the crease because of the lack of brightness. "Borderline unusable in natural daylight" another declared.

Some believe it wasn't his daily driver because it allegedly didn't show any apps nor touch the screen itself. Except the clip shows him swiping up with his thumb and the screen moving.

A dim viewpoint

When it comes to answering the question of why the screen is not super-bright in the interview, there are quite a few possible reasons for it. Some more obvious than others.

For a start, the red carpet is the worst place to judge a display on a device. We're talking about an area that is very brightly lit, with a different light characteristic than daylight, so that the stars can be filmed by the broadcast cameras.

This is a ton of light, and any consumer-grade device will have trouble competing with that situation. It also doesn't help that the broadcast cameras are set up to use this light so that the humans it sees look great, not necessarily a light-emitting device like a smartphone screen.

The second and most obvious reason is that Ternus didn't have the brightness turned up in the first place.

Whipping out the iPhone Duo in an off-the-cuff moment is different from a choreographed PR exercise which would've stuck the brightness as high as possible. It's probable that a prepared moment would've "fixed" the environmental lighting too so that the iPhone Duo looked perfect.

A multi-layered problem

Then there's the iPhone Duo display itself. We know it's using many layers of glass and other trickery to try and hide the inevitable crease, and that affects how the display appears to others, especially when it's someone viewing at an angle.

Apple's use of nano-texture is also at play here, since it's an etched texture designed to scatter light and to minimize environmental glare. It's not a one-way effect, as it does marginally soften the image of the iPhone Duo's OLED panel.

The iPhone Duo has many layers of glass - Image Credit: Apple

It also means that the contrast is affected when there's more environmental light to compete against. Under bright lights, the screen will look more grey and washed out than if you looked at the same screen in a dark room.

The decision to go for a matte display for the iPhone Duo was for consumers to have a better experience under normal usage. A glossy screen, as used by rivals, would look bright and make it more attractive for sales, but it would be a detriment for everyday use.

Under such extreme viewing conditions, it's completely understandable for the iPhone Duo to not be presented perfectly in Ternus' hands.

After all, the bright light there was to make the stars the awards were about shine brightly.

items.title: Musk doesn't get to just walk away from his Apple lawsuit
items.summary: Elon Musk filed to have his App Store dispute with Apple dismissed, but crucially not the simultaneous one with OpenAI. Now the judge is demanding to be told what's going on.
items.content_html:
Elon Musk filed to have his App Store dispute with Apple dismissed, but crucially not the simultaneous one with OpenAI. Now the judge is demanding to be told what's going on.

Musk's suit was a nonsense one claiming that Apple basically rigs App Store charts and features to favor its partner OpenAI's ChatGPT, and exclude X's Grok. It was entirely and demonstrably baseless, but Musk persisted, until he didn't.

On September 14, 2026, Musk filed to have the case against Apple dismissed. As AppleInsider noted, there were many unanswered questions and it was far from clear why Musk had done this.

Now according to Politico, OpenAI wants Musk and X to be compelled to explain the dismissal request. OpenAI filed this request as an emergency motion and the court has accepted it.

Consequently Judge Mark Pittman has now ordered Musk to produce any and all agreements he may have made with Apple to settle out of court.

The court order requires Musk's X and SpaceX firms to respond no later than noon on September 17. The judge also says that Apple is allowed to file a response by the same deadline, but is not compelled.

It's not clear yet what can happen after that deadline, or even whether Musk will actually be truthful about the reasons. That's because he has previously been accused of destroying and withholding evidence.

While it's also still not clear whether Musk and Apple settled out of court, it is clear why OpenAI is fighting the dismissal request. Unless OpenAI can get itself dismissed from the case as well, it will be facing two significant legal battles at the same time.

Alongside this nonsense one against Musk, OpenAI is facing the much more serious and seemingly substantiated accusation of trade secret theft from Apple.

items.title: Apple Reference Image is a mammoth effort to combat AI-edited photos
items.summary: Apple has explained how it has made Apple Reference Image as secure as possible, so you definitely know that the iPhone photo you're looking at hasn't been edited with AI.
items.content_html:
Apple has explained how it has made Apple Reference Image as secure as possible, so you definitely know that the iPhone photo you're looking at hasn't been edited with AI.

Apple Reference Image was introduced alongside the iPhone 18 Pro as a form of digital negative for an iPhone photo. It is billed as a way to prove that the image appears the same as it was when it was first taken, and that it isn't an AI-generated or edited shot.

On September 15, Apple Security Research published a post explaining how Apple Reference Image keeps the process as secure as possible. Creating proof of an image being unedited is one thing, but maintaining that level of authenticity against bad actors is another problem entirely.

AI-generated and edited images are getting too difficult to distinguish from the real thing, Apple writes. Photorealism of an image is no longer sufficient to establish a photographs veracity.

It's a problem that's quite tough to deal with, especially since modern camera systems use image-processing algorithms before the first viewable image is produced. To certify that an image is accurate, Apple says it needs a "chain of trust" for the sensor and that computational photography software.

However, existing approaches based on the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) standard add the provenance metadata after the point of capture. This allegedly makes it vulnerable to compromise in editing, defeating the object of the exercise.

Apple also warns that the C2PA approach attaches images to a public identity, creating a privacy risk for people in dangerous situations.

Apple believes that its answer is more secure, thanks to the integration of security throughout the photography chain and beyond into Private Cloud Compute.

Proving images

Apple Reference Image works to meet three core requirements.

First, semantic authenticity, meaning a reference image must show what the sensor captured. Any transformations of image data must be publicly verifiable.

It also must be resilient to compromise, such as anyone tampering with the camera sensor, jailbreaking the iPhone, or from cryptographic attacks. Images should also be revokable if it does eventually get compromised.

Lastly, the reference image must preserve privacy, even from Apple. Observers should not be able to determine if any pair of reference images were taken on the same device at all.

Semantic authenticity

To prove what the sensor shot, it isn't enough just to sign the raw values collected from the image sensor. Those values don't provide a visible image and need processing beforehand.

Rather than wait for the image to be processed before signing, Apple's approach starts from a secure boot of the sensor into a specialized reference camera mode.

That mode says to cryptographically sign pixel data immediately after capture, as well as preventing the sensor firmware from modifying it further. This is to prevent injection or tampering attacks before the operating system receives the pixel data.

Sensor-produced metadata is also signed at the same time. For those metadata elements that are beyond the sensor itself, such as digital zoom levels, the Secure Enclave signs the values.

The iPhone 18 Pro's camera has many updates for 2026. Apple Reference Image is just one of them.

Signing also ignores the basic timestamp process used by other systems for a more sophisticated approach. This involves creating a lower and upper bound on the capture time from Apple's cryptographic timestamp service.

Developing the image as a secure digital negative into one that is a user-visible reference image involves Private Cloud Compute (PCC). The image is uploaded to PCC, which handles the demosaicing, tone mapping, and compression that the iPhone usually performs after capture.

This work is performed in a way that can be verified by experts as not altering the negative at all, by checking the software. PCC production builds are also recorded in an "append-only, cryptographically tamper-proof transparency log."

Compromise resilience

The semantic authenticity explains that the system was built to withstand operating system-level and sensor bus attacks. However, other threats are also being managed as part of the system's design.

This includes hardware attacks that could even involve removing the sensor from the iPhone.

When the image sensor is initialized at the factory for the first time, it creates a cryptographic signing identity, with its public key recorded. The Secure Enclave also creates a separate signing identity, with the two identities bound in the device manifest.

This makes it possible to check that the sensor and Secure Enclave are on the same device. This platform information is added to the digital negative, with PCC able to validate the pairing.

Cryptographic attacks were also considered, with Apple implementing a system to be as "quantum secure" as possible. That is, able to resist attacks aided by quantum computing.

The last signature on a reference image is a composite post-quantum signature that combines RSA-3072 and ML-DSA-87.

Lastly, since even Apple admits that no security system is perfect, there's a revocation system to pull individual photos, and images from a specific sensor.

PCC creates a confidence score at the time of making the digital negative, based on the characteristics of raw sensor output. The photo GUID, sensor ID, and the confidence score is sent to a companion service before signing the developed reference image, updating a running score for a sensor.

If a sensor with a low score is revoked, PCC will not sign its images.

Photographer privacy

When it comes to maintaining the privacy of the photographer, Apple has shifted away from the usual concept of a photographer or institution vouching for an image using their credentials. Instead, Apple wants photographers to be able to remain anonymous, but keep the image verifiable.

Since images are signed by Apple's signing service after being validated by PCC, this eliminates the need to identify anyone behind producing the image.

The privacy properties of PCC also prevent Apple from accessing image data, much like how Apple Intelligence data is processed on its servers.

The revocation service does keep a private record of photo GUIDs and associated sensors. However, it doesn't have access to image data, and also actively prevents public access to the record.

Network visibility is also limited where possible. Timestamping requests happen over Oblivious HTTP, preventing the timestamping service from learning the IP address of the requesting device.

Calls to revocation and signing services also occur only from within PCC, with minimum information shared for those services to operate.

To Apple, the entire Apple Reference Image combines its combination of hardware and software capabilities, all to make a verifiable photograph for newsrooms and users to be confident hasn't been faked with AI.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: three-year upgrade, compared
items.summary: After three years, iPhone 15 Pro Max owners are likely to consider upgrading to the newest version. Here's how the iPhone 18 Pro Max fares against its 2023 counterpart.
items.content_html:
After three years, iPhone 15 Pro Max owners are likely to consider upgrading to the newest version. Here's how the iPhone 18 Pro Max fares against its 2023 counterpart.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple's latest premium model of smartphone, if you ignore the iPhone Duo. As the top of the line in many respects, it's what consumers wanting the ultimate iPhone will get, especially if they value photography and videography.

However, it's also three years after the introduction of the iPhone 15 Pro Max. That was a notable release for making major changes to the camera setup.

Three years is about the time smartphone owners will consider upgrading to a newer model. That means iPhone 15 Pro Max users will be having a good, long look at the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Here's how the two models compare, and if a three-year upgrade is worth it.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Specifications

Specifications iPhone 18 Pro Max iPhone 15 Pro Max
Starting Price (launch) $1,299 $1,199
Dimensions 3.07 x 6.43 in, 8.75mm thick 3.02 x 6.29 in, 8.25mm thick
Weight (ounces) 8.78 7.81
Processor A20 Pro A17 Pro
Storage 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB 256GB, 512GB, 1TB
Display type 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR, ProMotion, always-on, 3,000 nits max 6.7-inch Super Retina XDR, ProMotion, always-on display, 2,000 nits max
Resolution 2,868 x 1,320 at 460 ppi 2,796 x 1,290 at 460 ppi
Biometrics Face ID Face ID
Connectivity 5G (Sub-6GHz and mmWave), Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Ultra Wideband Gen 2, USB-C (USB 3) 5G (Sub-6GHz and mmWave), Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3, Ultra Wideband Gen 2, USB-C (USB 3)
Rear Cameras 48MP Fusion Main with variable aperture, 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide, 48MP Telephoto with 8x "optical-quality" zoom 48MP Main, 12MP Ultra Wide, 12MP Telephoto with 5x optical zoom
Front Camera 18MP Center Stage 12MP TrueDepth
Battery (Video playback) Up to 45 hours Up to 29 hours
Colors Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy Black Titanium, White Titanium, Blue Titanium, Natural Titanium

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Physical Dimensions

When Apple launched the iPhone 15 Pro Max, it was the first model to adopt a titanium frame instead of stainless steel. It was a sizable device at 6.29 inches by 3.02 inches to hold its 6.7-inch display.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a larger device, built to contain its 6.9-inch display. It's also made from an aluminum unibody frame, reused from the iPhone 17 Pro.

That matters when you have to deal with a physically larger smartphone. At 6.43 inches tall and 3.07 inches wide, the newer model is slightly bigger overall.

That also translates down to the thickness, at 8.75mm for the iPhone 18 Pro Max and 8.25mm for the iPhone 15 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Rear and side views

As for weight, the iPhone 18 Pro Max tips the scales at 8.78 ounces, versus 7.81 ounces for the iPhone 15 Pro Max. That's almost an ounce difference between the models.

The button selection changed with the iPhone 15 Pro, as the physical mute switch was changed for an Action button to go alongside the volume and side standby. The iPhone 18 Pro Max adds Camera Control, which gives users more immediate access to camera app features.

The other major physical evolution is the camera bump. While the iPhone 15 Pro Max has a square bump in one corner, the iPhone 18 Pro Max goes for the Camera Plateau that spans the width of the device.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Display

The iPhone 15 Pro Max had a 6.7-inch Super Retina XDR OLED display. With a resolution of 2,796 by 1,290, it had a pixel density of 460 pixels per inch, like most other iPhones the company sells.

Apple also included ProMotion support to 120Hz, along with an always-on mode for the display. There was also the Dynamic Island, some software camouflage for the camera cutout at the top of the screen.

The brightness was 1,000 nits for typical usage, with HDR content peaking to 1,600 nits. You could also see 2,000 nits if you used it in bright sunlight.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a bigger display at 6.9 inches, while still being a Super Retina XDR screen. That size also means a larger resolution at 2,868 by 1,320, but the pixel density is the same at 460ppi.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: The new display is brighter in the 18-gen model, while Dynamic Island has become even more useful.

ProMotion is still in use, as well as the always-on capability and the Dynamic Island. However, the Dynamic Island has been improved and is now capable of showing three Live Activities.

Brightness is up, however. The 1,000-nit and 1,600-nit levels are the same, but the 3,000-nit outdoor brightness is an improvement.

The 2 million-to-one contrast ratio has survived the generations, as have True Tone and Wide Color (P3) support.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a larger screen and certainly better in some respects, but the iPhone 15 Pro Max still holds its own.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Cameras

The iPhone 15 Pro Max brought with it a major change for Apple's camera system that was of high interest for content creators.

The 48MP Main, 12MP Ultra Wide, and 12MP Telephoto was a good trio, complete with LiDAR, however the Telephoto used what was referred to as a Tetraprism lens. The system, which helped bend light within a limited space, enabled Apple to provide a 5x optical zoom on that model, while the non-Max version stuck to a 3x zoom.

Three years later, the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a triple 48MP system. The upgrade also involved a name change, so they were known as Fusion Main, Fusion Ultra Wide, and Fusion Telephoto.

While the resolutions are up in the 18 generation, the Telephoto has not quite been kept the same.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: The latest model's rear camera plateau.

The five-times optical zoom has been turned into an eight-times "optical quality" zoom. Really, it's a 4x optical zoom, but it can be cropped and made to be as if it's an 8x optical zoom, a trick Apple uses to make the Main Fusion camera have a 2x "optical quality" zoom, too.

The bigger change for 2026 is the variable aperture system in the iPhone 18 Pro Max's Fusion Main camera. It can adjust in stages between f/1.48 and f/4.0, so photographers have mechanical control over the depth of field.

This is a change that will appeal to photographers and videographers, as they now have more control for more creative shots. While computational bokeh is still here, there's at least the option to experiment with the real thing.

Pro Controls are also being introduced to adjust the aperture, the shutter speed, and white balance, as well as provide a histogram.

The changes to the iPhone 18 Pro Max also extend to things like smart focus tracking and Apple Reference Image, for those who want to prove an image is genuine and not an AI edit.

For video, both cameras have Dolby Vision 4K, though the 18 Pro Max goes up to 120fps against 60fps on the iPhone 15 Pro Max. Again, Cinematic Mode with 4K Dolby Vision is better on the newer model at 60fps, versus 30fps.

Both benefit from Action Mode at 2.8K Dolby Vision at 60fps. Spatial Video survives at 1080p 30fps, though while Slo-mo on the iPhone 15 Pro Max managed 1080p 240fps, you have the 4K 120fps option on the newer device.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: The new variable aperture system.

The introduction of the iPhone 15 Pro Max also brought with it a bunch of professional-aimed additions, such as ProRes video support at 4K 60fps with external recording, ACES, and Apple Log.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max goes further again, with Pro Control, smart focus tracking, Dual Capture, ProRes RAW, and Genlock.

Apple included stereo recording in the iPhone 15 Pro Max, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max goes with a studio-quality four-mic array. The newer model also has Audio Mix and wind noise reduction.

The front camera of the iPhone 15 Pro Max is a 12MP TrueDepth array used for Face ID, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a new 18MP Center Stage camera. That upgrade means you can switch from portrait to landscape orientation shots without rotating the iPhone itself.

There's also Center Stage support as well as smart focus tracking and Time-lapse video with 4K Dolby Vision for that front camera.

Both the front and back cameras have received a lot of attention from Apple. Content creators will probably be willing to upgrade on the power of these changes alone.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Processing and Performance

Chip-wise, the iPhone 15 Pro Max was a milestone for Apple's mobile processing in its own right. The A17 Pro was the first 3-nanometer smartphone chip.

The A20 Pro is also a milestone, as it's the first using a 2-nanometer process.

Both chips have a six-core CPU in a familiar 2-performance, 4-efficiency configuration, though the newer one runs faster. Apple claims in its marketing that the A20 Pro's CPU runs 50% faster than the A17 Pro in the iPhone 15 Pro Max.

Joining each are GPUs, with a six-core version in the A17 Pro, seven in the A20 Pro. The A20 Pro's GPU also includes Neural Accelerators in each core, which help with AI tasks.

Speaking of AI, Apple has gone from a 16-core Neural Engine in the A17 Pro to a Dual 16-core Neural Engine in the A20. That means 32 cores of AI-processing silicon, as well as those Neural Accelerators.

Apple also has a vapor chamber cooling system in the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The iPhone 15 Pro Max simply doesn't have this element, so the A20 will do better when it comes to sustained processing.

The initial benchmarks for the A20 chip are starting to roll in before release, and they indicate that users can expect a big jump in performance. It's said that users can detect a 15% change, so it's certain that this will be noticeable this time around.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Geekbench 7 single-core benchmarks

The initial published listings show the A20 as scoring 4,006 in single-core Geekbench 7 tests. By comparison, the iPhone 15 Pro Max's A17 manages 2,532, giving the A20 Pro a 58% improvement over time.

On to multi-core, and the A20 manages 11,460. The iPhone 15 Pro Max's listing states it got to 6,865, giving the A20 Pro a 67% advantage.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Geekbench 7 multi-core benchmarks

Then there's the GPU figures, which should change based on both improvements to the cores and underlying technology, as well as the extra core in the A20 Pro.

The A20 Pro scores 62,302, which is massive against the 23,238 of the iPhone 15 Pro Max. That's a 168% change over three years.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Geekbench 7 Metal benchmarks

You should also bear in mind that these benchmarks don't take into account AI processing. The iPhone 15 Pro Max is considered the base model for Apple Intelligence support, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max will also support Apple's newest models.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max will benefit from both the increased available cores of the Neural Engine as well as those GPU Neural Accelerators.

Yes, you can certainly benefit from Siri AI on the iPhone 15 Pro Max. It will just be an awful lot more responsive for local processing on the newer smartphone.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Connectivity

The iPhone 15 Pro Max uses Wi-Fi 6E as well as Bluetooth 5.3. There's also a second-gen Ultra Wideband chip and Thread, as well as NFC on the rear for Apple Pay.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max switches over to the Apple-designed N1 wireless chip and improves connectivity to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.

iPhone 18 Pro Max

Apple's iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch OLED display and is powered by an A20 Pro chip.

Buy at T-Mobile
Buy at Verizon

While both support 5G on sub-6GHz and mmWave bands, the iPhone 18 Pro Max does so using Apple's C2 modem. Apple claims this will help improve both efficiency and speed when using cellular networks.

On the physical side, the iPhone 15 Pro Max debuted with USB-C, running at USB3 speeds of up to 10Gbps. The iPhone 18 Pro Max hasn't changed this element at all.

There's satellite-based services on both models, including Emergency SOS via satellite and Roadside Assistance via satellite. There's also Crash Detection, which will work with Emergency SOS via satellite if you have an accident in a cellular blackspot.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Power and Battery

Apple's largest smartphones tend to have massive amounts of battery life. This certainly hasn't changed for the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The iPhone 15 Pro Max was introduced as capable of up to 29 hours of video playback for locally stored video. This dipped to 25 hours for streamed video playback.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max, on the other hand, can muster up to 45 hours of local video playback from a single charge, or 40 hours if you stream it.

This is a monumental upgrade, and makes the iPhone 18 Pro Max more useful for all-weekend usage without needing to baby the battery life too much.

When it comes to charging, both support MagSafe with Qi2 and Qi support as well.

The iPhone 15 Pro Max can get up to 50% charge in 35 minutes using a 20W adapter and USB-C charging. The iPhone 18 Pro Max can get a 50% charge in about 15 minutes when paired with a 60W adapter or higher using USB-C.

This isn't directly comparable, but it's safe to say they can recharge quickly.

On the iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple also says it can manage 50% charge in 30 minutes over MagSafe when using a 35W adapter.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Capacity, Color, and Pricing

The iPhone 15 Pro Max started at $1,199 with a 256GB capacity storage, with options for 512GB and 1TB also available.

It was sold in four colorways: Black Titanium, White Titanium, Blue Titanium, and Natural Titanium.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: The colors of the iPhone 15 Pro generation.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at a slightly higher $1,299 with 256GB of storage. Options are also available for 512GB, 1TB, and a new 2TB option, if you're prepared to spend $2,499.

It comes in Black, Silver, Glacier, and Burgundy

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Which to buy

To owners of the iPhone 15 Pro Max, the iPhone 18 Pro Max represents three years of improvements from Apple. A lot can happen in one year, let alone three.

The main changes are in the cameras, with that variable aperture system being the biggest of the lot. While tetraprism attracted photographers and videographers, the ability to change the aperture will have a similar effect.

iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 15 Pro Max: Colorways of the iPhone 18 Pro Max

Battery life is also a sizable improvement, as is the processing performance. The latter is especially so as the industry moves towards more onboard AI processing tasks.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the ideal upgrade for the user of the iPhone 15 Pro Max. However, they may not necessarily feel the need to do so.

The A17 Pro is still more than capable of number crunching without necessarily feeling slow by modern standards. It's not blisteringly fast, but it's not lagging behind just yet.

People who need better imaging for professional uses will be drawn to the new model. But as it stands, there's no shame in sticking to the iPhone 15 Pro Max for another year.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders off to a surprisingly slow start
items.summary: Whether it's because of the economy, better supply than normal, the looming iPhone Duo, or Apple's unusual opening of pre-orders on a Saturday, very few iPhone 18 Pro models are showing any shipping delays as of an hour after preorder start.
items.content_html:
Whether it's because of the economy, better supply than normal, the looming iPhone Duo, or Apple's unusual opening of pre-orders on a Saturday, very few iPhone 18 Pro models are showing any shipping delays as of an hour after preorder start.

Following their launch on September 9, 2026, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models are now available for pre-order. But they did not sell out immediately, as is more normally the case.

By 08:30 ET, half an hour after pre-orders opened, no color or configuration of the iPhone 18 Pro showed any shipping delays at all in the US. They remained available to be delivered on Friday, September 18.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max fared better, but not by much. None of the 1TB or 2TB versions are delayed whatsoever.

But the first model to see any delay was the iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB one in burgundy. Shortly after 30 minutes, it slipped from September 18 to between September 29 and October 6, which is around a week and a half to two weeks later.

By the one-hour mark, that model was delayed a further week, showing as October 6 to October 13. The 512 burgundy model initially slipped to between September 24 and September 29, but by 09:00 ET it too was October 6 to October 13.

Similarly, the glacier color iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB slipped to up to two weeks after half an hour, and so did the same configuration in silver. It's now showing October 6 to October 13, and the black 512GB model is September 24 to September 29, while it's still September 18 in silver.

The black iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB model also slipped to September 24 as its earliest delivery date.

These are all figures for the US Apple Store and there has been a difference overseas. In the UK, for instance, all but the 2TB version of the burgundy iPhone 18 Pro slipped back to September 24.

What's happening

Moving to Saturday to open pre-orders, in order to not be on 9/11, has surely had an impact as people's schedules and availability will be different. There is also the fact that it's not yet possible to pre-order the iPhone Dou, so buyers may be waiting for that model.

Or there is the fact that the global chip shortage has made prices higher. Plus the global economy is such that discretionary spending is reduced.

However, it is also possible that Apple has done a better job of predicting early sales demand and managed to produce sufficient quantities to meet it.

items.title: Apple Intelligence could be the key to cram Face ID into future iPhone Duo
items.summary: A new report obviously predicts that Apple wants to replace the iPhone Duo's existing Touch ID with Face ID as soon as possible, and suggests that Apple Intelligence might help.
items.content_html:
A new report obviously predicts that Apple wants to replace the iPhone Duo's existing Touch ID with Face ID as soon as possible, and suggests that Apple Intelligence might help.

Touch ID is easily the most apparent compromise in the iPhone Duo, and Apple has had to go back it because of that model's slim chassis. It was not physically possible to fit the usual Face ID components into that space.

Now Bloomberg has made the obvious prediction that Apple will be working to add Face ID to future generations of the iPhone Duo. But it's also suggested that AI could be part of the solution.

The claim is that Apple Intelligence could ultimately help with not just the iPhone's computational photography, but also all of its image processing. So Apple could in theory use less sophisticated depth-sensing camera systems and let AI take up more of the processing role.

That would then presumably mean that the physical Face ID components could be smaller. The prediction is that this will not happen until the third generation of the iPhone Duo, by which time the report also expects the model to gain a telephoto camera.

This is also an obvious prediction and the third generation iPhone Duo is sufficiently far off to make it an easy guess. But the suggestion of AI augmenting the hardware components would fit Apple's unusual ability of entirely controlling its software and hardware together.

items.title: Apple's 'vintage products' list now includes the final 21.5-inch Intel iMac
items.summary: The age of the Intel Mac is coming to an end in every sense, as Apple now classifies the last 21.5-inch Intel-based iMac as a "vintage product."
items.content_html:
The age of the Intel Mac is coming to an end in every sense, as Apple now classifies the last 21.5-inch Intel-based iMac as a "vintage product."

In 2019, Apple updated the aging Intel iMac with eighth-generation Intel processors and new AMD Radeon graphics cards. It shipped in the same slim chassis Apple introduced back in 2012, and Apple still offered then-outdated options like the 1TB Fusion Drive.

It was already a mediocre upgrade in its own right, but the arrival of Apple Silicon the following year made it even less desirable. Now, macOS Golden Gate has ended software support for Intel Macs, and the 2019 21.5-inch iMac has made its way to Apple's "vintage products" list.

Apple considers a product "vintage" when it stopped distributing it for sale more than five years ago but less than seven years ago. The company provides service and parts for vintage products for up to seven years, assuming the necessary parts are available.

Once a product hasn't been sold new for more than seven years, it's then classified as "obsolete." In short, the 2019 21.5-inch iMac is still eligible for repairs from Apple and its authorized service providers, assuming the required parts are available.

While the 2019 21.5-inch iMac will officially be obsolete in 2028, meaning repairs will no longer be offered, that doesn't mean the computer won't be serviceable at all. Apple's older Intel iMacs feature upgradeable storage, RAM, and a socketed CPU, assuming you're willing to remove the display with the proper tools.

Software-wise, the last 21.5-inch Intel iMac will likely forever be stuck on macOS Sequoia, though Apple is still expected to release security updates through 2027.

items.title: GM caves, CarPlay won't be cut from gas-powered vehicles
items.summary: It wasn't all that long ago that GM's executives called taking CarPlay out of vehicles a "Jobsian" move. They've caved to public pressure, and the option is present in some 2027 gas vehicles.
items.content_html:
It wasn't all that long ago that GM's executives called taking CarPlay out of vehicles a "Jobsian" move. They've caved to public pressure, and the option is present in some 2027 gas vehicles.

The interface is expected in the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks. Based on the description by GM, it comes with gauges, hands-free driving, and more. All of this feels like Apple's new CarPlay interface.

There will be 60 inches of screen space in the new vehicles, with a screen for videos for the front-seat passenger.

GM hasn't offered the interface in electric vehicles for three years, and it's not clear if the option will be restored. Gas-powered cars retained the option, but there were plans in motion to pull it from there as well.

Apple is apparently part of the retention.

"We listen to our customers, what they want, and, going forward will still have projection in our trucks," said GM's executive director of connected apps and services Michael Wahlstrom. "We worked with both Apple and Google to develop a new split screen that includes the projection experience right next to the native experience."

The news was first revealed by Bloomberg, but not by Mark Gurman.

items.title: Siri AI is built to be replaceable by Claude or ChatGPT
items.summary: Substantial code references found in the latest iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate betas reveal that Siri AI is already set up to let users replace it with alternatives.
items.content_html:
Substantial code references found in the latest iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate betas reveal that Siri AI is already set up to let users replace it with alternatives.

The same developer who found watchOS code for the then-unannounced Readiness app has now found that Apple has prepared Siri AI to be almost completely replaced. Frequent leaker "pdfu" has shown not only code references, but also demonstrated using Claude in place of Siri AI.

iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate have private hooks that let apps add Siri Extensions and replace Siri AI's server backend with third-party models.

First, here's Claude running as a Siri Extension using the Model Delegation API in App Intents. Claude can appear in Siri's "Ask" pic.twitter.com/OXKHQ4hDY8

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 13, 2026

While not officially available yet, this is similar to how iOS and macOS can already use ChatGPT as an extension to Siri. Since 2024, if Siri couldn't answer a query, users could let it be passed to ChatGPT.

It was previously reported that there would be other such extensions, but while this new discovery includes Claude as well as ChatGPT, it is a more extensive option. When enabled, Claude or ChatGPT appear in Siri's "Ask..." menu, for instance.

According to "pdfu," these as-yet private hooks use the Model Delegation API in App Intents. When done this way, responses are shown prefixed with the word "Claude," but otherwise looking exactly like the new Siri AI interface.

Reportedly, if a request requires interaction with iOS or macOS, such as setting alarms, Claude relays that to Siri AI to complete it.

That means Siri AI remains the AI model that has access to users' personal data. But it also means that users could take advantage where an alternative such as Claude is better able to perform a given task.

Consequently, if a user has to elect to use Claude and knows that is what is being used, then this is potentially a good way to extend the functionality of AI on Macs and iPhones.

And here's an app extension replacing Siri AI's server model with GPT-5.6 Terra. It uses the Inference Providing protocol in Model Manager Services.

GPT-5.6 receives Apple's native Siri planner prompt and tool definitions. It can make tool calls that perform system actions, and pic.twitter.com/cz88kyq3io

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 13, 2026

There is a second part to this, however, which appears to show that Siri AI could be entirely replaced by ChatGPT. It can be made the default for all AI requests, but more than that, does not use Siri for its responses, and can access system functions.

Both of the demonstrations shown appear to be running on a Mac. OpenAI recently added the ability for ChatGPT to control Messages on a Mac, but Apple's security prevents it doing the same on an iPhone.

However, these code references and demonstrations are Apple's own work. They appear to be fully functional, just hidden from regular users for now.

It's hard to see Apple approving OpenAI having this level of access without Siri AI guardrails. But then even if Apple does let ChatGPT in, there is no reason to use it, and every reason to distrust it.

items.title: What iPhone Duo doesn't have, and what compensates for those losses
items.summary: The iPhone Duo manages to balance some compromises with unique features that make it a much better option than the iPhone Air. Here's what you don't get in the folding iPhone, and what offsets those losses.
items.content_html:
The iPhone Duo manages to balance some compromises with unique features that make it a much better option than the iPhone Air. Here's what you don't get in the folding iPhone, and what offsets those losses.

The iPhone Air created a fork in Apple's lineup that gave users a premium choice that wasn't "pro." However, some users complained that it may have cut too many corners to achieve its thin and light design.

For the past year, the conversation around iPhone Air has been primarily about what it lacked. While I believe the iPhone Air is a perfectly fine iPhone, I think the iPhone Duo did a much better job addressing user needs.

The iPhone Air battery complaints were overblown, it basically has the same battery life as the iPhone 16. The camera also was just fine, if nothing to brag about.

iPhone Duo, however, gives more back than what had to be taken away. I've already detailed why I believe the iPhone Duo camera system will be more than adequate for most users, but I wanted to discuss its compromises a little more broadly.

The thing is, there's really not much to discuss.

iPhone Duo isn't just thin for the sake of it

If you're someone that complains about the iPhone Air, you might comment that the thinness was completely unnecessary. I've seen people suggest that a bit more thickness for grip and additional battery life would have made it a better iPhone.

iPhone Air is the spiritual precursor to iPhone Duo

The thinness was the point.

Apple built iPhone Air because it could. It was clearly a testbed for what was coming next.

The iPhone Duo is even thinner than the iPhone Air, though still not thinner than the iPad Pro. That thinness means it is impossible to include a long-range telephoto camera.

Apple also likely struggled to include the necessary sensors for Face ID on multiple sides of the device. There just wasn't enough space, and every bit of space was needed for the two batteries.

However, the thinness serves a purpose with iPhone Duo. When open, it's thinner than iPhone Air at 0.21 inches versus 0.22 inches, but when it is closed it's 0.44 inches, which is only a tenth of an inch thicker than an iPhone 18 Pro Max.

iPhone Duo isn't the thinnest foldable out there, but its titanium frame, 10-layer inner display, and 24-hour mixed-use battery life contribute to that. Apple could have likely gone thinner or lighter, but at the sacrifice of build strength and quality.

Since this is the first folding iPhone from Apple, the company likely went more conservative than it had to. Expect future models to push the limits of what's possible, as some foldables are so thin they're nearly too thin for a USB-C port.

iPhone Duo has MagSafe after all

At one point the rumor mill seemed confident that the iPhone Duo wouldn't have MagSafe capabilities. That would have meant an absence of magnetic charging and ecosystem accessories.

iPhone Duo has MagSafe, but it's going to need new accessories

Obviously, that didn't come to pass. I had initially been concerned that the device's weight or shape might be awkward for some stands, but that also wasn't an issue.

The MagSafe on iPhone Duo is different than on other iPhones — it appears to lack the bottom stabilizing magnet. Or, at the very least, previous MagSafe accessories were made with a longer iPhone in mind.

If you've collected multiple MagSafe batteries and wallets, you might be out of luck with the iPhone Duo. Sure, most will still attach, but the bottom will stick out from the foldable.

This is one of the few most notable compromises users should be aware of when buying an iPhone Duo. Accessory makers will need to design new MagSafe wallets and batteries that fit the new squat design.

Looking around the web, some have already begun offering such accessories. There appears to be enough space for a wallet that can hold a credit card, it'll just need to rethink the size and magnet placement.

Existing stands and accessories that use only the circle part of the MagSafe connection will work fine. I'll be testing all of the accessories in my home and reporting on what's still okay, what doesn't fit, and what's plain weird.

iPhone Duo's lack of Face ID

The lack of Face ID is going to be a sticking point for some people. Apple clearly couldn't get the technology to work in a thin device that had multiple active sides in use.

Apple chose a Touch ID sensor for iPhone Duo since Face ID would have proven difficult

Face ID is more secure than Touch ID, by Apple's own admission, but that doesn't mean it isn't secure. It's just another biometric tool for unlocking your device.

For those that don't like Touch ID, find it cumbersome, wear gloves a lot, don't have all their fingers, or are left-handed, there's a solution. Those that own an Apple Watch will have their device authenticated automatically.

I'll need to test this feature, but I'm certain there are protections that prevent people from unlocking your iPhone just because they're standing next to you. If not, then use this feature at your own risk.

Convenience always compromises security in some fashion.

For me, Touch ID is fine. I've been using Touch ID on the iPad mini for years without issue.

Compared to the ease of use and higher security of Face ID, the use of Touch ID is a compromise. However, I wouldn't consider it a deal breaker by any means.

iPhone Duo's inner display will crease

The final compromise I wanted to point out was the inner display. Given that the display needs to fold, it can't be made of super tough, thick, and durable glass.

No matter how much you baby it, the iPhone Duo inner display will develop a crease

Instead, it's made of "a custom polymer," which is Apple speak for plastic. It's ten layers with tons of stuff in between, including two sheets of glass, but the top layer is nano-textured plastic.

The hands-on with iPhone Duo at Apple Park revealed that the inner display looks and feels great. In spite of the nano texture and non-glass material, Apple seems to have made it look and feel like any other iPhone display, though with a matte cover.

I have the iPad Pro with nano texture, and it's never been a problem for clarity or visibility. In fact, it's quite remarkable how usable it is in broad daylight, which makes me excited for the iPhone Duo.

However, there's no beating physics. The nano texture and display layers will help mitigate the development and visibility of a crease over time, but it's going to develop.

There is no way to know how durable the iPhone Duo inner display is, and I doubt anyone tried to break one during the iPhone event. Don't worry though, YouTube and TikTok will soon be filled with people needlessly breaking the product.

I'm confident that Apple's display will be one of the better ones on a foldable, but that doesn't mean it won't crease. It's the nature of the product, and a compromise made no matter which foldable you buy.

Where iPhone Duo exceeds expectations

Considering an iPhone Air cable connection is limited to USB 2.0 speeds, charges slower than iPhone 17 Pro, has a lesser battery life than similarly-priced iPhones, and has a very limited camera system, I wasn't sure what to expect from iPhone Duo. My concerns were rendered mostly moot by the product reveal.

Many parts of iPhone Duo were unexpected

As I've said previously, the camera system appears to be more than enough for most people, even ones coming from an iPhone 17 Pro. It may not have the new fancy variable aperture or Fusion Telephoto camera, but those systems only benefit the smallest percent of photos.

The following features more than make up for the few compromises iPhone Duo has.

  • A20 Pro with vapor chamber cooling
  • 24 hours of mixed use between both displays
  • 50% recharge in 20 minutes with 60W adapter
  • IP68 splash, water, and dust resistance
  • Under display FaceTime camera
  • Apple Pencil with USB-C support
  • New StandBy features
  • Smart Take, Duo Preview, and Duo FaceTime
  • Custom iOS for new aspect ratios
  • A real blue color

The iPhone Duo is an iPhone through and through. It's still Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and sports the C2 modem.

The safety features Emergency SOS, Roadside Assistance, and Messages via satellite are still here. Crash Detection also works on iPhone Duo.

I'll admit, I was skeptical that the iPhone Duo would ever make it to market. Apple managed to keep actual hardware from leaking, mostly, even though rumors basically got every spec and measurement correct.

Nothing about my previous musings has changed. Foldables are an expensive niche. They seek to solve a problem that doesn't really exist, but are launching in a market that's craving more than just a roundrect glass panel.

Apple Vision Pro is Apple's future, while foldables are the present

Spatial computing is the more likely future. Given how slow development is there, good foldables can have their day.

The Android foldables I interacted with until now felt slapped together. Android was bolted on, and apps rarely, if ever, acknowledged the form factor (Yes, iOS developers will need to update).

It was easy for me to be skeptical given what had come before. It's still easy. That said, Apple has succeeded in making me interested in a foldable.

Now, time will only tell if it is truly a great experience and one I will want to keep having through future generations of the product.

items.title: Samsung holds Apple to $250 per iPhone Duo display in three-year deal
items.summary: A leaker with a reasonable track record has sketchy details of what they claim Samsung's iPhone Duo display deal is with Apple.
items.content_html:
A leaker with a reasonable track record has sketchy details of what they claim Samsung's iPhone Duo display deal is with Apple.

It was already known that Samsung makes the displays for the iPhone Duo, and also that the screen company had an exclusive deal. Apple was seemingly forced to accept the arrangement because no other firm was able to supply the required screens.

Now according to leaker Instant Digital posting on the Chinese social media site Weibo, the deal is a three-year one. It's to cover the current iPhone Duo and future models during that time, and they say Samsung is charging $250 per panel.

Previous reports say that Apple's other main display manufacturer, LG Display, does not yet make folding screens. BOE makes them for Huawei, but reportedly Apple considers those inadequate, plus it regularly has problems with that company's reliability.

While overall component prices are known to have risen for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, previously Apple was offering Samsung and LG Display around $70 per display panel.

The interior screen on the iPhone Duo is of course vastly more complex than the one on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, so it's unsurprising that it would cost considerably more to manufacture. But it means that the display is an unusually high proportion of the costs of manufacturing, representing around an eighth of the iPhone Duo's retail price.

That $250 price does not include any costs of assembly or testing. It also presumably only applies to the interior screen, as the leaker does not mention the exterior or front screen.

Instant Digital has a reasonable reputation for accuracy. They may well be one of the people Apple's Greg Joswiak was thinking of when he said that it was unfortunate that some leakers had got details of the iPhone Duo.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Case size, design, dimensions

For the Apple Watch Ultra 4, Apple opted to use a tried-and-true design. As a result, the new model is effectively identical to the preceding Apple Watch Ultra 3.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Apple hasn't made any changes to the design of its top-of-the-line smartwatch. Image Credit: Apple.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a bulky smartwatch, with a flat display and curved edges. It has an Action button and Digital Crown on the side of the titanium enclosure. The latest Apple Watch Ultra has kept the 49mm case size of preceding models.

Still, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is slightly heavier. In Natural Titanium, it weighs 63 grams, while the Black Titanium version has a weight of 63.1 grams.

The Apple Watch Ultra 3 in Natural Titanium weighed 61.6 grams, while the Black Titanium version weighed 61.8 grams. The new model is less than two grams heavier.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 still uses sapphire crystal and ceramic for the front and back, respectively. Meanwhile, the main enclosure is made from 100% recycled titanium on both the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Ultra 3.

There's no change in terms of dimensions, either. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 measures 49mm by 44mm, with a thickness of 12mm, matching that of the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

Durability remains unchanged as well with the Apple Watch Ultra 4. The new model is certified for MIL-STD 810H durability, IP6X dust resistance, and water resistance of up to 100 meters (328 feet).

As for the display, both the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Ultra 3 have an Always-On LTPO3 wide-angle OLED screen. It has a maximum brightness of 3,000 nits.

For both Apple Watch models, the display area is 1,245 square millimeters, with a resolution of 422 by 514 pixels.

While the titanium casing and OLED display haven't changed with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, the hardware inside certainly has.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Processing hardware, performance

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 boasts the new S11 chip. It has a power-efficient, always-on processor with a new Secure Exclave. Inside, an audio buffer securely manages raw audio for processing.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Apple Watch Ultra 3: The S11 chip offers better performance and enables new Apple Intelligence features. Image Credit: Apple

Apple's S11 chip also has a faster CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine, all derived from the A20 Pro chip. The S11 CPU has two efficiency cores and a Neural Accelerator. Its last-level cache is 50% larger than the one in the S10 chip.

Its quad-core Neural Engine similarly offers increased bandwidth compared to the preceding generation. Additionally, the S11's single-core GPU offers increased bandwidth and compute, says Apple. The company calls the S11 its most powerful wearable chip yet.

All that extra power isn't just for show, either, as the Apple Watch Ultra 4 supports all-new Apple Intelligence and Health features.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Health features

Health-focused functionality has always been a staple of the Apple Watch Ultra, and the fourth-generation model is no exception. Relative to its predecessor, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 features a redesigned health sensing system.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Apple has added multiple health-related features, including a new Readiness score.

Apple says the new hardware is built on its innovative health sensing foundation, and that it improves three core elements.

The larger electrode surface area enables better skin contact during electrocardiogram (ECG) readings. Additionally, redesigned photodiodes were arranged into a ring to capture light more efficiently.

Larger green LEDs, with improved power efficiency, are used to support accurate heart rate measurements during the day. Combined, these changes allow for improved optical sensing.

Relative to Apple Watch Ultra 3, the new health sensing system in the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers higher-frequency, continuous heart rate data. This metric serves as a key indicator of overall health, says Apple.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 takes background heart rate readings every five seconds. That's 60 times the frequency of readings on the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

Apple's upgraded health sensing system also samples heart rate variability (HRV) twenty-four times more frequently than the previous model. This means the Apple Watch Ultra 4 samples HRV every five minutes.

HRV indicates how well someone's body responds to stress. Higher values are typically associated with better overall recovery, says Apple.

HRV is included in the Overnight view and a new Daytime view, both of which are in the Vitals app on the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Apple conducted a study comparing the Apple Watch Ultra 4's health sensing system to other wearable products. The company used an ECG chest strap as a reference.

Over a thousand participants engaged in a variety of activities for the study, including cycling, HIIT workouts, running, and more.

The study found that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 has "the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable." Improved sensors aren't the only new experience with the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

The Readiness experience uses the wearer's recent activity, vitals, and sleep data to offer an idea of their body's overall capacity during the day. A numerical score and description guide the wearer on the amount of physical activity they should do.

The Readiness score can be viewed via the Health app on iOS, and it updates during the day. The Health app on iPhone has been redesigned as well.

Apple Intelligence uses Apple Watch data to offer custom suggestions via the new Insights tab. Dynamic, user-tailored recommendations appear in other areas of the app.

Apple Watch Ultra 3

The Apple Watch Ultra 3 has an Always-On Retina display and up to 3000 nits of brightness.
Buy at Amazon
Buy at T-Mobile
Buy at AT&T

There's also a Health Age feature, which explains how the wearer's health metrics, like VO2 Max and sleep data, compare to their actual age. Apple's new Longevity tab uses iPhone and Apple Watch data to assess the user's overall health.

Additionally, the iPhone and Apple Watch can be used together to conduct specific tests, like VO2 Max assessments.

During the test, the iPhone camera records your movements as it displays a video of what to do. Simultaneously, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 records health-related metrics.

The upgraded sensors in the Apple Watch Ultra 4, coupled with more frequent heart rate measurements, make the watch the go-to option.

In terms of Health features, Apple Watch Ultra 3 is no slouch, either. It offers blood oxygen monitoring and hypertension notifications, but the Apple Watch Ultra 4 simply has more to offer.

The same is true when Apple Intelligence features for the Apple Watch are taken into account.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Apple Intelligence

Though the Apple Watch Ultra 3 already offers a limited number of Apple Intelligence capabilities, such as the Workout Buddy feature, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 takes things to the next level with Audio Intelligence.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Audio Intelligence delivers three new features for the Apple Watch. Image Credit: Apple.

Audio Intelligence encompasses multiple sound-related capabilities available on the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

As a new accessibility feature, Apple's new top-of-the-line smartwatch includes sound recognition. This lets the watch detect sounds like sirens, doorbells, crying babies, and more. The end user receives an on-screen notification for each detected sound.

Live Rewind lets you replay sentences detected by the Apple Watch Ultra 4 in the form of a text snippet. It only goes back fifteen seconds, but it's enough to let you catch a book recommendation or list that you might have missed. No audio recordings are created or stored.

Siri Recap can summarize conversations had while wearing the Apple Watch Ultra 4. The feature is entirely optional, though. Apple's commitment to user privacy is still a priority with Audio Intelligence.

The company emphasizes that audio files are not stored anywhere, and that the audio data is not accessible, even to Apple. It's only used to provide summaries of conversations when you allow it to.

Live Rewind and Siri Recap both require Siri AI, meaning you'll need an iPhone 16 or newer to take advantage of these two features. Audio Intelligence will be available later in 2026, with Siri Recap and Live Rewind arriving in beta later in 2026.

In terms of Apple Intelligence features, it looks as though the Apple Watch Ultra 4 can run circles around its predecessor. Battery life has been greatly improved as well.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Battery life, connectivity

Apple says the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is equipped with a larger battery. Coupled with the S11 chip and new health sensing system, it lets the Apple Watch Ultra 4 achieve a remarkable 50 hours of battery life. That's up from 42 hours on the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Apple claims the Apple Watch Ultra 4 can last up to 45 hours in the new Max Extended workout mode. Image Credit: Apple.

As for workout tracking with full GPS and heart rate monitoring, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is capable of delivering up to 18 hours of battery life.

Extended Workout activates Low Power Mode and turns off the always-on display. During the workout, running form metrics are unavailable in this mode.

In exchange for this limited functionality, the new Extended Workout mode delivers up to 25 hours of battery life.

There's also a new Max Extended workout mode, which offers up to 45 hours of battery life.

Apple says Max Extended Workout turns on Low Power Mode during workouts and disables alerts, splits, and select metrics. This mode also turns off the always-on display.

The Extended Workout and Max Extended Workout modes are not available on the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

In Low Power Mode, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 can last up to 84 hours, up from 72 hours on the preceding model. Apple says the Apple Watch Ultra 4 can gain up to 18 hours of use from a 15-minute charge, again up from 12 hours on the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

In terms of connectivity, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 includes support for Wi-Fi 4 as well as Bluetooth 5.3. While Bluetooth and Wi-Fi support remain unchanged from the Apple Watch Ultra 3, Apple did make a minor satellite-navigation change.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 supports GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou. However, Apple has dropped support for GLONASS, which was available on the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

With GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Ultra 3 receive position information using the L1 and L5 bands. These satellite-navigation systems use CDMA (Code Division Multiple-Access) to transmit signals.

GLONASS, meanwhile, utilizes a different transmission architecture, called FDMA (Frequency-Division Multiple Access). On the Apple Watch Ultra 3, it delivers position information over only the L1 band. Support for GLONASS is not available with the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Though Apple did not explain why it removed GLONASS support, its absence may actually have improved GPS accuracy and battery life. The hardware no longer uses energy for single-frequency GLONASS signals.

Apple claims the Apple Watch Ultra 4 has "the most accurate on-device GPS in a sports watch." This is according to an August 2026 study that compared the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to "industry-leading dual-frequency GPS sports watches" available at the time.

Overall, the absence of GLONASS support likely won't mean much to potential Apple Watch Ultra 4 buyers. The seemingly improved GPS accuracy, however, might appeal to those considering the new model.

Connectivity details aside, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 offers 8 hours of extra battery life. With all the new health-related enhancements and performance, it's the obvious choice if you're looking to upgrade. Pricing hasn't changed, either.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Apple Watch Ultra 3: Pricing

Apple offered the Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $799. It was sold in Natural and Black Titanium color options.

The same is true for the Apple Watch Ultra 4, which is also priced at $799 in both Natural and Black Titanium variants.

items.title: You need to join the Siri AI waitlist before you can use it
