items.content_html:
Siri AI is open for business, but interested users will need to join the queue before Apple lets them in the door. Here's where it is, and how to sign up for the list.

Apple's new Siri AI features aren't automatically available after installing iOS 27. If you're interested in trying, you must first request access through a waitlist.

To join the waitlist, you need to meet certain criteria. This includes having a compatible iPhone, setting your language to English, and meeting age and country requirements.

If you do meet the criteria, you can join the waitlist by following the steps below.

  1. Ensure your iPhone is updated to iOS 27
  2. Open Settings
  3. Tap Siri
  4. Tap Try Siri AI (beta)
  5. Follow the prompts

As the name implies, joining the waitlist doesn't guarantee immediate access to Siri AI. Even users who were using Siri AI in the beta need to rejoin the waitlist.

Apple is rolling out the features gradually, so users may have to wait before Siri's new capabilities become available. Some have been let in nearly immediately, while others are still waiting, hours later.

Once access is granted, the iPhone will notify you that the new Siri features are ready. Any additional models or resources required to run the features will then be available to download.

Apple has used waitlists for major AI launches before, including the initial Apple Intelligence rollout.

items.title: Apple's Xserve may return with Nvidia tech
items.summary: Apple is reportedly considering a return to the server market it left when it abandoned Xserve, but this time incorporating the future M8 Ultra chip, fully integrated with NVLink Fusion technology.
items.content_html:
Apple is reportedly considering a return to the server market it left when it abandoned Xserve, but this time incorporating the future M8 Ultra chip, fully integrated with NVLink Fusion technology.

While Apple already makes its own servers in Houston, it is reportedly looking at making a rack-mounted server product for wider distribution.

The rumored product line is said to include two main configurations. One would feature two M8 Ultra chips, while the other would use four of the still-unreleased processors.

As part of the technology assessment, Apple is said to be considering using NVLink Fusion. That is high-bandwidth, low-latency connective technology that allows companies to plug chips and AI accelerators directly into Nvidia's advanced data center infrastructure.

Originally limited to just Nvidia hardware, the company has recently opened up the technology for others to license and use.

Nothing will hit the market before 2029, and it's not clear exactly who can buy what will be ridiculously expensive hardware. A report by The Information on Wednesday morning discusses that plans are to sell to "AI developers, other businesses and governments," with the latter two the main target of the original xServe hardware.

New CEO John Ternus is said to have been a backer of the project, when it sprung up inside Apple about a year ago. And it would need his full backing, as the effort would have to source expensive components, in epic quantities, well before the project starts.

Apple refuses access requests to its self-manufactured Private Cloud Compute hardware. The company has also partnered with Google and Amazon for cloud capacity in the past.

Apple and Nvidia

The report paints Apple's relationship with Nvidia as "frosty," but I disagree with that sentiment. It's been beyond that, and publicly, it's been downright frozen.

That relationship started with Steve Jobs in 2001. It led to defective solders, poor performance, and allegations of trade secret theft made by Jobs.

Apple support for Nvidia hardware has been poor for over a decade. There were drivers for Nvidia cards in Intel hardware, but that effectively stopped after the 5,1 Mac Pro stopped shipping, and before Apple popularized eGPU enclosures in 2016.

By 2019, video card driver support was killed, for good.

But, perhaps, there's a thawing now. Money talks, after all.

"We would always rather sell something than nothing," Dion Harris, Nvidia's senior director of high-performance computing and AI infrastructure, said in an interview. Reportedly, Harris declined to comment on whether Apple is an NVLink Fusion customer, but said that "Apple has always been a great customer and partner of ours."

That partnership and customer status may be recent. Apple was said in March 2026 to have bought $1 billion on Nvidia hardware for research. Specifically, it was said to have purchased 250 Nvidia NVL72 servers at a cost of between $3.7 million and $4 million each.

For a look back at the Xserve, Jeff Geerling has an excellent saga about refurbishing the 20-year-old G5 version of the hardware. Notably, this hardware was used in the Virginia Tech "Big Mac" cluster in the summer of 2004, after launching in 2003 with towers.

And I saw them again about four years later at the university's surplus auction, where they turn up from time to time to this day.

items.title: 'Widow's Bay' leads Apple to multiple record-breaking Emmy wins
items.summary: Apple TV has again won the most awards at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards, plus it has become the most awarded streamer ever.
items.content_html:
Apple TV has again won the most awards at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards, plus it has become the most awarded streamer ever.

Apple TV had already won 20 awards during the first nights of the 2026 Emmy Awards, in the chiefly technical categories. But now it has brought that up to 29, making it the most awarded network of the year for the second time running.

Its wins at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards also mean that Apple TV broke records just with "Widows' Bay," which saw:

  • Most wins for a freshman comedy in Emmy history
  • Most wins for a comedy in a single season
  • Most performance wins of any series in 2026
  • Hiro Murai getting the first-ever comedy directing win for an Asian

Plus Apple TV is not only the most Emmy-awarded network, it reached that in the seven seasons since its 2019 launch. That also makes it the fastest streamer to accomplish this.

"Reaching milestones like these feels incredibly special for all of us at Apple," said Matt Cherniss, Apple TV's head of programming in a statement, "but what makes it especially meaningful is what it represents: the extraordinary storytellers we have the privilege of working alongside."

"There is nothing like the power of a great story to capture our imaginations, surprise us in unexpected ways, and remind us of what connects us," continued Cherniss. "'Widow's Bay,' 'Pluribus,' and 'Slow Horses' have done exactly that. Congratulations to all of the artists honored and thank you to the Television Academy."

  • Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series: Matthew Rhys

items.summary: Apple Intelligence summarizing of HomeKit Secure Video cameras is very useful, but you'll have to really want it as it's tied to iCloud+ plans that start with a single camera for $10 per month.
items.content_html:
Apple Intelligence summarizing of HomeKit Secure Video cameras is very useful, but you'll have to really want it as it's tied to iCloud+ plans that start with a single camera for $10 per month.

As iOS 27 comes out of beta testing, Apple has updated a support document that reveals the pricing for its Apple Intelligence features in the Home app. Specifically, the promised Apple Intelligence automatic summarizing of security video comes with certain iCloud+ costs and limits.

  • 2TB iCloud+ includes 1 camera for $10 per month
  • Apple One Family subscriptions include one camera at $39.95 per month, including 2TB of storage
  • 6TB iCloud+ includes up to 2 cameras for $30 per month
  • 12TB iCloud+ includes up to 5 cameras for $60 per month

There is no support for the feature on either the 50GB $1/month tier, or the 200GB $3/month one.

Apple's support document also links to a short list of compatible cameras. That list is on the Apple Store and is of six cameras, ranging from $145 to $250.

Not the only benefit

The iCloud+ tiers do not only offer camera support, of course. The feature was launched to provide additional storage over the really tight 5GB that Apple provides each customer.

But it also now includes features such as Hide My Email and iCloud Private Relay, both for privacy purposes.

Those features come as standard with any iCloud+ plan. What Apple is still not saying is precisely how iCloud+ users will benefit with the ability to use Apple Intelligence features more.

That's because Apple does say that in the future it will impose usage limits on Apple Intelligence features such as photo editing or Siri AI. "Increased access to such features will be available for a fee," says the support document.

It's not clear whether this means Apple will also provide Apple Intelligence-only plans. But the company has previously confirmed that iCloud+ users on the 2TB tier or above will have more access.

items.title: It's not clear why Elon Musk has filed to dismiss App Store favoritism suit
items.summary: Elon Musk has moved to dismiss its lawsuit against Apple regarding the App Store given preferential treatment to OpenAI over xAI's apps. There are unanswered questions.
items.content_html:
Elon Musk has moved to dismiss its lawsuit against Apple regarding the App Store given preferential treatment to OpenAI over xAI's apps. There are unanswered questions.

The court filing on Monday, September 14 is pretty sparse, other than the request to dismiss. It's not yet clear if there's some kind of settlement, or if Musk has decided his case is baseless.

OpenAI was named in the suit as well. Notably, it's just Apple that Musk is asking the court to remove from the case, and OpenAI will need to fight two major legal battles with industry titans at the same time.

Apple and OpenAI were sued by Elon Musk's xAI, now owned by SpaceX, due to alleged anticompetitive practices. The trial hasn't been going well for Musk so far, as it was accused of destroying and withholding evidence previously.

The suit alleging preferential treatment has been sketchy from the beginning. As Musk's own Grok noted when asked by a social media user, other companies other than OpenAI have been on the top of the App Store.

DeepSeek was in the App Store top spot in January 2025. Perplexity followed on July 18, 2025. Both happened after the June 2024 OpenAI and Apple partnership.

Further complicating the suit, app data aggregator SensorTower has also noted that Grok was on the peak App Store spot on February 18, 2025 and February 19, 2025 after Grok-3 was made free.

The case has been moving at a snail's pace since it was brought on August 2025. In May 2026, SVP of Software Engineering Craig Federighi was brought in as a document custodian.

Current Apple CEO Tim Cook was also requested as a custodian, but that was denied.

And, more recently, a judge has ruled that Elon Musk's emails must be entered into the record. It's still not clear what has triggered Musk's request.

We have reached out to Apple and X corp for more details. We are not expecting a response from either, but a return call from Apple is more likely.

items.title: Apple updates AirPods as iOS 27 adds customizable EQ

items.content_html:
Apple's latest AirPods firmware lands alongside iOS 27, giving users more control over how their headphones sound.

On Monday, Apple released a firmware update for AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2. The build number is 9A350.

The firmware arrives alongside iOS 27, which brings new audio controls to several AirPods models. The update expands customization options in Apple's latest operating systems.

iOS 27 adds a customizable equalizer for AirPods Max 2, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods 4. Users can manually adjust low, mid, and high frequencies instead of relying on Apple's default sound profile.

Equalizer settings are stored on the AirPods themselves, allowing the selected profile to carry across connected devices. The settings also display the current audio waveform while users adjust each frequency range.

Monday's firmware update will install automatically for users when AirPods are plugged into their charging case, if applicable, and connected to an iOS device. There is no manual installation method for this firmware update.

How to check your AirPods firmware version

AirPods users can check the current firmware for their audio accessories by accessing the Settings app on their iPhone or iPad.

  • Select General
  • Select About
  • Select the AirPods you wish to view

A menu will appear showing relevant device information.

items.title: macOS Golden Gate is here and Siri AI is its remarkable best
items.summary: After months of beta testing, Apple has released macOS Golden Gate. As always, it's a mix, but there are great improvements and Siri AI is mostly fantastic.
items.content_html:
After months of beta testing, Apple has released macOS Golden Gate. As always, it's a mix, but there are great improvements and Siri AI is mostly fantastic.

Fantastic is a strong word but apart from a few aspects that are still startlingly poor in it, Siri AI deserves the description. Up to now, Siri has really been an iPhone tool as it was cumbersome and slow on the Mac, and simply not as useful there.

Going straight into Siri AI

Now, incorporated into Spotlight so that it is always a keystroke within reach, Siri AI transforms the macOS Siri experience entirely. Gone is the tiny popup in a corner, and what's most welcome is that the need to stop typing and wait for Siri's response is gone too.

With macOS Golden Gate, you can call up Spotlight, ask Siri AI to find that email where you told that charity some dimensions for an advert some time, and carry on working. Faster than you could ever find that three-year-old email, Siri AI is back with exactly the answer.

But truly, the fact that you can carry on working while it looks is as transformative as what it is now capable of doing. The Spotlight/Siri AI black dialog box does pop up in the middle of your screen, but you can drag it out of the way and carry on typing in your document.

I now use Siri AI whenever I want something that I know is on my Mac somewhere, whether that's a document or an email. That charity advert email was urgent but the request came when I was deep in the AppleInsider podcast, so having it just be found for me so quickly was such a boon.

I could've just searched my calendar, true. But then I asked Siri AI to find the concert tickets in one of my email accounts, and it did.

Similarly, there's a concert I was due to see last year but it was cancelled, then rescheduled, and when I suddenly worried that I'd missed the new date, it was Siri AI that said no, you're fine. You're seeing Dar Williams at this date and at this location, it told me, plus here's the email with the tickets.

On and on it goes, I'm practically at the stage of calling up Siri AI before I've finished thinking what I want. If I sound like an evangelist, it's because I now am and specifically so because macOS Golden Gate has made Siri AI so readily prominent and useful.

I would say that I no longer Google anything, I just ask Siri AI, but that's not entirely true. Siri AI doesn't always find what other AI services do, so I still keep Claude around.

Although while there presumably can't have been much work done by Apple on what it calls Siri's World Knowledge, I'm now only rarely finding Siri AI's answers to be wrong. For some reason that was different at the start of the beta test.

Siri AI always gives short answers to questions and usually they're too short.

However, for some unfathomable reason, Siri AI responses are still intentionally limited to how much you could say in a single breath. I'm sorry, but I have no particular concern over whether Siri runs out of breath or not.

So if I'm searching for something that I know will need more detail, then I will again turn to Claude.

Plus, let this be a public service announcement: Siri AI finally works with Apple Music. But only on the Mac.

Until the last moments of the macOS Golden Gate beta test, and still in the final iOS 27 beta, Siri AI would claim to be able to add Apple Music tracks to playlists. But it would then work only just often enough that you would keep trying.

Most of the time, the gigantic majority of the time, Siri AI would say it couldn't find the playlist you said. Even if just before, you had asked it to play that playlist and it had done so without complaint.

Apple Music and Siri AI integration was, and still is on iOS, enraging, partly because of how patronizing it could be. If you keep asking, Siri AI will eventually apologize for your confusion, as if it's you who is getting this wrong.

It was not chance that means Siri AI has been coded to say "I won't respond to that" when you tell it just precisely what you think of it.

I should be ecstatic that it's now working on the Mac, but on the one hand, I almost always use that particular feature on the iPhone while driving. And on the other, there was a whole twenty minutes during one beta release where it worked on the iPhone too.

You can't believe the surprise when Siri AI finally added an Apple Music track to a playlist, like it always said it could.

There weren't that many people using the beta, compared to how many will now have it. But Apple has the problem of convincing those beta users to try this feature again.

Which feels like an own goal because Apple already had the much greater issue of getting anyone to try Siri at all. Apple broke Siri two years ago and then left it like that.

Deep breath.

Nonetheless, you must try Siri AI on macOS Golden Gate and by itself, it is the reason to upgrade. You have to get on a waitlist, though.

What else macOS Golden Gate brings

Saying that Siri AI is the reason to upgrade is of course a way of stressing just how good it is, when it's good. But this is also close to strictly accurate as the only major update to macOS this time is Siri AI.

So there are refinements to Liquid Glass, for instance, but they're really just a sop to the vocal minority who don't like that redesign. Apple can tell you that there are now controls for adjusting just how liquid its Liquid Glass features are, for instance, and it's not lying.

There is a slider to adjust how liquid Apple's Liquid Glass design is, but it doesn't make much difference.

But you have to whack the slider fully to one way or the other to really distinguish any difference at all. Since I'm fine with Liquid Glass, I tried this, shrugged at it, and never went back.

Your mileage may vary, as alongside this overall Liquid Glass slider, there are improvements to individual elements. So you could fill your time trying out variations on the appearance of Dock icons, and that might be worth it.

I say that particularly because while I haven't done any of that appearance fiddling, Apple has. This is just me, I realise, but somehow through the betas I kept mistaking the Preview icon for the Keynote one.

L-R: The Keynote icon, the original Preview icon, and the final Preview one.

They're not even really that close, but something about them kept tripping me up. Then in the latest betas and now in the final release, Apple has changed the Preview icon and I no longer choose the wrong one.

Mind you, I prefer the previous Preview icon.

One other change during the beta process was that Apple removed the old toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. I wondered at first whether that meant everyone was stuck with Apple Intelligence, but there is now a Turn Off Siri control which may do the same thing.

There's no toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence any more, but there is one for turning off the whole of Siri. Though you won't want to.

I wouldn't know, really, because originally I wasn't bothered by Apple Intelligence in any sense of the term. And now, specifically because of Siri AI, and specifically because of how it is on the Mac, Apple Intelligence is part of my daily workflow and I've no interest in turning it off.

Shortcuts

While Shortcuts works across the iPhone and iPad as well, I am most often creating them on the Mac. Which means my second favorite aspect of macOS Golden Gate is how Apple Intelligence has changed Shortcuts and made it much quicker to use.

Unfortunately, for several years, the Shortcuts action to open a Safari tab group has failed on the Mac. It works fine on the iPhone and the iPad where it's of little use, since you're already tapping on the screen.

The new Shortcuts app is very good at clearly saying what a Shortcut it creates will do. Except it sometimes doesn't do anything of the sort.

On the Mac, it would be so convenient to press a keystroke or tap a Stream Deck button to switch between Tab Groups. And you were supposed to be able to do exactly that.

You still can't, and some time in the last few beta test versions, Apple implemented a kind of solution. It removed the Open Tab Group action from the Mac.

It's unfathomable why Apple couldn't make this work when it added the action. But it's more unfathomable why the new Shortcuts will pretend to do it.

Seriously. It's a bad part of what is otherwise a brilliant feature, which is the Apple Intelligence version of Shortcuts.

Previously, Shortcuts would offer countless actions that you could drag into a list which it would then work through. You can still do this and you can still create complex Shortcuts by hand.

You can tell Shortcuts what you want in plain English and while far from flawless, it is remarkably good at creating just what you need.

But Apple has added Apple Intelligence to the simple plus button that gets you started. Once you click that, Shortcuts just asks you what you want to do, then it does the job of choosing the actions and assembling the Shortcut to do it.

There are times when this is so good that it is amazing and you think you'll never fashion a Shortcut manually again. For instance, there's a timing thing I need for the AppleInsider podcast and I could never quite work out the math, but Shortcuts did it immediately.

Yet there are times, such as with the Safari tab groups example, where Shortcuts will tell you that it has done what you asked. It will present a concise list of what precisely that Shortcut will do for you, even if it will not do anything of the sort.

It's not surprising that there are limits, of course. But it is surprising that there are these failures when sometimes Shortcuts will display an error message saying it can't do a particular thing.

So Apple Intelligence in Shortcuts is like Apple Intelligence in Siri AI. Absolutely fantastic, except when it's pants.

Shortcuts can build reasonably complex Shortcuts automatically.

Nonetheless, the ability to incredibly quickly make at least basic Shortcuts by just saying what you want, that's transformative. More Mac users will get into Shortcuts because of this.

And while I actually enjoy writing Shortcuts for myself, most of the time now I do start by asking for what I want. Of the last 20 Shortcuts I've made, all of them started this way, although 5 failed.

That's still a 75% success rate, which could well be better than my own.

Surprisingly useful Photo tools

Just as on iOS 27, macOS Golden Gate also includes Image Playground and it has been improved. I've not used it once for serious work, but I do see the improvement.

That's because for some reason, and who knows why, I once asked the previous version to create an image of five clowns carrying a horse. That version gave me too few clowns, too many horses, and looked dreadful.

That image is actually far better than the first betas of Image Playground could produce. But I asked for five clowns, not seven.

Trying the same prompt now, the image is vastly better and there is only one horse. But for some reason there are seven clowns. They seem happy.

What I have used for actual work is the way that Photos can now edit images. I was making a poster for my YouTube channel and needed more space for the text, so I had Photos extend my image.

It took moments. Open Photos, pop the image in, choose Edit, Tools, Extend, and then drag across where you want to widen the image. It didn't take Photos much longer to do the job.

And let this be proof of how well it did it. I did this a couple of months ago and staring at my YouTube channel, I cannot now remember or even guess which poster I did this with.

That was a real use-case for me, but I did experiment with the other photo manipulation features early on in the beta and originally had more limited results. So limited that I did not again try reframing a shot to move someone's eyeline, and I did not try to erase large sections of the image ever again.

Don't look at my silly hat, look at the Apple Store to the right. There was a whole person there before. And my own right arm is AI-generated.

Until just now. Trying it out again now, the results are staggeringly better than they were.

It must depend on the shot, but I had one of me and my wife in Vancouver, sitting against a glass partition in that city's great Apple Store. For obvious privacy reasons, I just now used Clean Up to remove my wife and I tell you, if we ever divorce, I'm going to use this instead of cutting up all our printed photos.

Clean Up removed her, and filled in the space not with some generic background, but what looks to me like what really was originally behind her. It has taken a sliver of an Apple Watch poster and recreated that, plus put some of those Apple Store wooden cube seats there.

But then I reframed it because for some reason I wasn't quite looking at the camera. It's like I thought I was a YouTube presenter or something.

There was only a slight reframing adjustment needed, but it did it. It did it with finer controls than there were and, most importantly for me, it did it so well that it truly looks like I was staring into the camera.

But to do that, I noticed that it filled in some more of the background around the edge of the frame. So I tried telling it to extend more and I chose the most difficult part.

In this shot, I am leaning into frame from the left, so I extended it out in that direction. And Photos made up my arm and jacket perfectly.

I'm still going to tell people to look into the lens, please. But what seemed like a toy at the start of the beta test is now a usable, potentially useful feature.

Writing Tools are a shrug, but a useful one

This bothers me because it's creating some material and I never imagined I'd do that. I'm certainly not going to be using macOS Golden Gate's Siri AI to write anything.

Although... It's now 31 years since Microsoft Word added red underlining for spell-checking and that means for three decades I've barely paid any attention to it. That's an exaggeration, but it's definitely true of the blue underlines you get when Word is bored and decides to make up grammar rules.

Yet during the beta test of macOS Golden Gate, I've been more conscious of Writing Tools. Never the actual feature, I don't think I've opened those more than once, but the gentle automatic underlining as I type has been rather good.

Once, Siri AI also went ahead and corrected the spelling in my document too.

Plus there was a time when, as I'm in England, I wasn't certain of the US spelling of a word. I called up Spotlight, asked Siri AI, and it told me I'd got it wrong, which was helpful.

Every time, too, I can type "Fix it" into Siri AI and it does, it amends my text. Once it just did that anyway: told me it was wrong, corrected it in my document and said "you're welcome."

Okay, it didn't say that, but it was still startling to see it happen. I don't understand why it did this that once, but even being able to ask it to fix the spelling of one specific word seems good to me.

Fantastic, staggering, and dreadful

You can tell I like macOS Golden Gate and you won't be remotely surprised to learn that I do not want to go back to macOS Tahoe. But it isn't all brilliant, and there are annoyances even beyond the peculiar problems with Shortcuts.

I say annoyances. Some are minor and actually I'm certain they are only because I'm writing this while still on one of the last betas. There's a bug right now about when you scrub through a video; the slider keeps snapping back to the start, for instance, and that will surely be fixed.

Or there is that great feature when you're saving a document and can click on the name of an existing one. That copies the existing name and you can just make some changes.

So I'll have video assets such as "Take 1" and can just replace that digit with 2 rather than typing out the whole name. That's been a thing on the Mac for as long as I can remember, but in the last betas it was working too quickly.

I would be in the Save dialog, move to a new folder, and find that my document title was immediately changed to that of something already there. It always seems to happen when I've taken the time to write a new document title, too, and that gets wiped out.

Similarly, a bug I've had that appears to still be here is that menus in Save dialogs won't always work. In Pixelmator Pro, for instance, I can't always specify that I want to export an image as PNG instead of JPEG because the menu flips back closed too quickly.

Of course the Phone app has separate audio controls from System Settings, although at least they are now under "Audio" instead of "Video."

But if there were one Mac thing I would wish Apple would fix... no, okay, one thing other than Shortcut tab group support, it is the Phone app.

This should be extraordinarily useful. To be able to make and receive calls on the Mac without getting out your iPhone, it should be so very handy.

But it does not work.

There has been one minor improvement. Originally it was that despite any other sound setting on your Mac, the Phone app had its own. It would sometimes even default to something you no longer had connected.

True, once you knew it did this ridiculous thing, you could change the audio setting. Once you also knew that to change anything to do with audio, though, you had to look under the Video menu.

This is now better. That same menu has been retitled Audio. Although while that lets me specify what microphone and speaker I want on one Mac, on another it won't. It just snaps back to whatever it was set to by default.

But it doesn't help even when you can set these. I have the correct microphone and speaker selected in it, but if I call someone, they cannot hear me.

I'd obviously like that to be fixed, please, and I struggle to understand why the problem hasn't been resolved yet. But then maybe I'm just a heavier phone user than most.

Only, since I am, I would also like to be able to answer or end calls with a keystroke or a Stream Deck button. As it is, I have to wait for the call notification to appear, then find the green answer button.

Even Keyboard Maestro clicks on that Answer Phone icon to no avail.

That notification is now appearing quicker than it did, so it's no longer the case that people have hung up before it's displayed. But clicking on that green answer button is a lottery because sometimes it just does not respond.

You could blame my hand/eye coordination, except for this. I went to the trouble of making a Keyboard Maestro macro and including in it a screenshot of that button.

Now I press a Stream Deck button, it launches that macro, Keyboard Maestro looks for the button, finds it, clicks it, and nothing happens.

I'd phone Apple to ask them about it, but...

Devils and details

The more you dig into anything, the more likely you are to find problems. I'm conscious that in the case of macOS Golden Gate, what are truly small irritations still manage to burrow under my skin.

I think you can rightly criticize me for that, it is surely a sign that I need to get out more. But perhaps it's also a sign of how important macOS is to me.

If you are a Mac user, it has always been astounding how much you can do with these devices. I've a relative who believes I am a computer geek because I'll spend 15 hours in front of my Mac, but to me that's not what I'm doing at all.

I'm writing articles, I'm editing video, I'm reading books, I am doing countless things that I need and enjoy and relish. A new macOS is just about the only thing that touches every part of that, every application, and every task.

So a new macOS is an enormous deal. And while I initially thought that Siri AI was the sole update in macOS Golden Gate, I do now see that there is more.

It's still the main update and it's still fantastic. But overall macOS Golden Gate is yet another example of how Apple makes you wonder why you put up with the previous version at all.

items.title: Apple brings smarter Siri and better health tracking to Apple Watch in watchOS 27
items.summary: watchOS 27 brings Apple's new AI-powered Siri, expanded health features, and smarter everyday tools to the Apple Watch.
items.content_html:
watchOS 27 brings Apple's new AI-powered Siri, expanded health features, and smarter everyday tools to the Apple Watch.

As anticipated, watchOS 27 didn't bring a massive overhaul to Apple Watch, but instead brought the device in line with the rest of the Apple ecosystem. This isn't surprising; Apple has been spending the last few years explaining its plans to do just that.

Here's what Apple brought to watchOS 27.

Siri AI

Apple made it clear that it would bring its new, improved Siri to Apple Watch at WWDC 2026. The goal is to provide personal, contextual artificial intelligence to an Apple Watch wearer.

Siri can now hold back-and-forth style conversations, which gives users the option to probe Siri for multiple queries in a row. A dedicated Siri app stores conversations across devices.

A dedicated Siri app allows you to revisit your conversations all in one place

And thanks to Siri's access to a user's personal data, it can search across Calendar, Mail, Messages, Notes, Reminders, and more. It can share flight details with family, play songs sent by friends, and add new goals for Activity Rings.

In addition to personal context, Siri also has broad world knowledge. This allows users to ask about nearly any topic, such as recipe ideas, wellness tips, and even transit schedules.

Health & Wellness

A redesigned Workout Buddy offers insights and gives users motivation based on fitness history, utilizing data insights based on progress, distance, and workout duration. And now Workout Buddy doesn't need your iPhone nearby, either.

Workout Buddy no longer requires your iPhone to be nearby

Indoor running is now more accurate, thanks to improved motion tracking algorithms. Users can accurately track indoor runs and walks from their wrists.

Perimenopause and menopause support has also been added. Users will receive alerts when cycle patterns are suggestive of perimenopause.

General improvements

A new one-tap gesture has been added in watchOS 27. Tapping your index finger and thumb together once allows you to select a widget in the Smart Stack.

Smart Stack suggestions have also been retooled. More widgets appear in the Smart Stack, including birthday suggestions, car locations, alarm changes, and more.

The watchOS Find My app has been improved in watchOS 27. Find Devices, Find Items, and Find People are now streamlined, making it easier to locate in a map-centric view.

Call Context gives users proactive information on their wrist while in a call. For example, if you call an airline, Apple Watch can proactively surface a confirmation code from Mail.

Other minor improvements include faster music playback, improved step synchronization across Fitness and Health apps, and battery optimization.

items.title: Why your iPhone Duo will inevitably develop a screen crease
items.summary: The iPhone Duo developing a crease over time is inevitable as the tides, and a matter of physics and engineering. Here's how and why that crease develops, and what Apple has done to mitigate it.
items.content_html:
The iPhone Duo developing a crease over time is inevitable as the tides, and a matter of physics and engineering. Here's how and why that crease develops, and what Apple has done to mitigate it.

In the run-up to Apple's folding iPhone, there was a lot of chatter about how Apple has "solved the smartphone crease." It's always been a silly topic, as there is no solving it, there is only postponing it.

It's an engineering problem on top of a physics problem. The physics are immutable.

What can be controlled is engineering tolerances, coupled with precise engineering, tailored to known stress points. It's about working around the issues of a hybrid screen, with the properties of both glass and plastic.

Plastic OLED and very, very thin glass layers

On its own, the OLED screen substrate is not rigid, and can bend and flex because it is essentially plastic. It too can break and tear, and is very soft, Because it is soft, it lacks what makes glass a good material for a smartphone touch surface.

Any type of glass, including Gorilla Glass, is a non-crystalline, amorphous solid. It's generally characterized by high chemical resistance, and a hardness which makes it a good smartphone touch surface, where the screen isn't.

Glass has poor thermal conductivity. And, it has a low coefficient of thermal expansion which makes it good for a smartphone screen.

Importantly, especially here, it is somewhat elastic. Especially when very thin.

To that end, folding smartphone glass is not one sheet. Ultra-thin glass, which is both a product name and a descriptor, is sandwiched in layers. Each layer is thinner than a human hair.

Each layer has with a coat of sliding adhesive. When the device is open and closed, this allows the layers to remain intact and slide very slightly across its neighbor. A thicker, single piece of glass would crack and shatter, versus the bend and slide

The hinge makes sure every fold is about the same, and optimized for minimal and even stretching of the glass.

This hinge means everything to the iPhone Duo screen

Extremely thin glass isn't new. Apple's glass partner Corning made Willow Glass in 2012, and has been selling it on rolls ever since.

At the time, it was used for static curved screens, long before the first folding smartphone, and basically at the dawn of the OLED era. The two combined has led to where we are now.

And, it will crease. Every folding screen will, even Apple's.

Fatigue failure and that crease

For years, there has been discussion of that crease in smartphones. It was very apparent on early smartphones with plastic screens because of the material properties of plastic.

Arguably, most failures will be from user drops and other impacts. That's not what we're talking about here, but a drop will aggravate a crease formation.

Progressive fatigue on that hinge point is the main factor behind obvious crease development.

Crush a can in the center, and bend it until it tears. That is a practical, accelerated demonstration of the same way that a crease in a smartphone develops over time.

Apple is not immune to remorseless physics. Engineering can mitigate physics somewhat, though. The hinge is a key factor.

I'm reasonably confident that Apple has engineered a hinge that will retain its tightness and regularity. The uniform and precise fold, each and every time, will limit the variables that need to be controlled to minimize fatigue damage, because the folds are uniform and the stress points are known.

Every material has a minimum bend radius where the material will fail, or take damage. I spoke about this briefly above, but the hinge keeps the glass on the correct side of that line with an arc, not strictly a bend.

But, still, over time, micro-cracks will emerge along the hinge point. And over time, the screen will start to delaminate just a bit.

All of this damage is accumulative. Fortunately, most screens, likely including Apple's, are rated to survive about 250,000 folds over a product's lifetime.

Some napkin math suggests that's more than 125 shut-to-open and back again cycles per day over five years.

Along the way, though, that accumulating damage will be visually and touch-evident at the point of maximum stress. That point is the center of the hinge.

That point is the crease. A crease, even on Apple's $2000 folding iPhone, is inevitable. It is a matter of time, and use.

Apple and engineering

Every single engineering problem is a compromise between physics, the material that can be used, the engineering you can bring to bear, and the cost it extracts to make the material. It's been long said that Apple over-engineers a problem.

I can't think of a problem that needs an "over-engineered" solution more than minimizing accumulated fatigue in a hinged material.

Apple has had seven years to look at competitors and see how their engineering has failed, and how it's been engineered around. That's a lot of flaming data to use, and make sure that your product doesn't crash and burn like that.

Apple has done well here, but how well it has done is up to time and contact with consumers. There are already concerns about the folding, and there are going to be the idiots in Apple stores who like to pound on demo hardware, which will accelerate those cycles.

Expect to see people opening and closing the iPhone Duo dozens of times in minutes, grinning like a fool when they do it and recording it on their own iPhones for social media cred. This isn't FineWoven where the problems were obvious, so don't rely on those videos for any measure of success or failure.

We're also sure that Apple will capture every single one of those units that gets pounded on at retail and test it to the point of total destruction, like they do.

Phones will be destroyed for YouTube clicks, and the folks with infant failures that do happen, will complain disproportionately loud on social media.

Enjoy your tech. Being concerned about the crease at this juncture is a waste of your time, like min-maxing your battery with operational habits that may or may not help is now.

While the crease is inevitable, there is no indication today that it is a show-stopper. The phones are designed to be used, they are designed to be open and shut, they are designed to get that Uber, to watch that video, to surf that site.

We still have hooks inside Apple Stores' service departments. Let us watch the numbers, let us figure out if it's a giant problem like the stage lights on the 13-inch MacBook Pro a few years ago, or the butterfly keyboard was. Let us figure out if it's a problem that deserves some non-hysterical watching and discussion like the orange iPhone turning pink for some folks with an coating misapplication at the factory in some early production units.

And, Apple replaced or fixed all of those actual issues.

Until then, ignore the folks that test to failure, and use your iPhone Duo. Report issues to Apple, and we'll let you know if there's a problem over time.

items.title: Apple rolls out tvOS 27 with support for video podcasts, improved audio
items.summary: Apple's tvOS 27 update brings a redesigned Podcasts app, better Apple Music audio, new accessibility features, and a handful of smaller improvements to Apple TV.
items.content_html:
Apple's tvOS 27 update brings a redesigned Podcasts app, better Apple Music audio, new accessibility features, and a handful of smaller improvements to Apple TV.

As you know by now, Apple TV updates are somewhat modest compared to other Apple products. That's especially true after the major Liquid Glass redesign introduced with tvOS 26.

Still, tvOS 27 has a few worthwhile additions, particularly for Apple Music and Podcasts users. Here's what Apple's rolling out to the Apple TV.

Podcasts gets a major overhaul

The Apple Podcasts app is getting one of the biggest changes in tvOS 27.

Apple has completely redesigned Podcasts for the Apple TV, adding a new sidebar that makes it easier to navigate through the app and browse shows.

The bigger change is support for video podcasts. Video podcasts are already supported on other platfroms, but tvOS 27 brings that experience to Apple TV.

Smart downloads are also coming to Apple TV. This allows podcast content to be downloaded automatically so that episodes are ready to play when needed.

Apple Music adds new audio features

Apple Music is getting a few improvements in tvOS 27, including support for Hi-Res Lossless audio.

Apple is also bringing AutoMix to Apple Music on both Apple TV and HomePod via tvOS 27. AutoMix uses transitions between songs to make playlists flow more continuously, rather than simply stopping one track before starting the next.

Accessibility improvements

tvOS 27 adds a long-requested accessibility feature with support for larger text.

Users can increase the size of onscreen text through the accessibility settings, making menus and other information easier to read from across the room.

Quality and performance upgrades

Of course, Apple has also been working to improve the overall experience of tvOS in this newest update.

Most notably, animations and app launches are smoother. Control Center is also more responsive.

How to update your Apple TV to tvOS 27

  1. On an Apple TV, go to the Settings, app
  2. Select System
  3. Select Software Updates
  4. Select Update Software

How to update your HomePod or HomePod mini

  1. Ensure your device is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS.
  2. Open the Home app
  3. Tap or click ...
  4. Tap or click Home Settings
  5. Tap or click Software Update
  6. If available, tap or click Update
